title: Who knew we would be obsessed with this screen?
author: engineering-AF7
selftext:
What are some things you are doing to control token spend? 

On my end, for repetitive complex tasks I am using Fable to come up with the result I want and to create the skill.  I then downgrade to a lower model to run the skill. 

https://preview.redd.it/ugtsidwngedh1.png?width=930&format=png&auto=webp&s=20b0de12383025091d3d0c7564ead49c7c213bb2

comments.author: magus_prime_x
comments.body:
I always keep the chat compact and avoid carrying unnecessary context for too long. 
For research, file searching, and early planning, I use a lower-cost model.
 Once the plan is complete, reviewed, and confirmed, I switch to the stronger model for the actual execution.

I also use at least two strong AI tools instead of expecting one to handle everything. 
For example, Claude can handle deep planning, visual judgment, documentation, and long project reasoning, while Codex can focus on coding, debugging, testing, and working directly inside the project or vice versa. 

Having one AI review the other’s work is also a great way to catch mistakes.
The prompt itself needs to be very specific: where the project is located, which files and folders it should work in, exactly what the task must do, what must not be changed, and which skills, tools, MCPs, or plugins it should use. I also include clear acceptance criteria so the AI can test its own work instead of guessing whether it is finished.

For bigger tasks, I split the work into focused stages: inspect first, create a plan, confirm it, execute, test, and verify. 
This usually gets the task completed properly within two or three attempts instead of wasting tokens through endless trial and error. If it still fails after that, I stop and investigate the root cause rather than repeating the same prompt.

replies.author: engineering-AF7
replies.body: Thank you, that is very helpful. The concept of for example having Fable in Claude Code create a plan and the let the very capable, but significantly cheaper GPT 5.6 implement it within Codex is something I will try.

comments.author: LiveBeyondNow
comments.body: A small tip ( aside from useful suggestions Magnus has) I use is to query a cheap model with a very small request. If you have a necessary query, even better, but the point is to start the 5hr clock about 2hrs before you “sit down to work”, that way your 5hr limit is reset sooner.  This doesn’t help with the weekly limits but I have also seen them not start until queried so I try to do the same on weekly resets.

comments.author: kruzibit
comments.body: I use fable to plan and spec then sonnet 5 to execute, then fable to review.

replies.author: engineering-AF7
replies.body: Makes total sense, I will do the same. BTW has anyone tried to define the model(s) a Skill should use for different parts of its work?

comments.author: Forexcalibur
comments.body:
I create slash commands called /endsession and /remember.  When the session has accomplished its work, the session covers a lot of ground, I’m at a good stopping point, or approaching compaction, I run /endsession and it updates claude.md, status.md, memory, and session handoff, including anything that future sessions will need to come fully back up to speed with context, makes sure everything is committed, and pushes to the remote git repo.  /endsession has instructions to keep the .md files small and organize subject-specific guidance and guardrails into downstream .md files the root files reference.

After that I /clear to clear the session, and then run /remember, which causes Claude to read up all of the aforementioned files, verify state, review the previous session’s transcript, and come fully back up to speed with context.

I regularly run these slash commands while I’m working to keep my sessions accurate with lean, sharp, recent, relevant context.
